name: molecular_geometry
doc:
MOLECULAR GEOMETRY - VSEPR shapes and angles, sealed (issue #11, 2026-10-16: reach, down the domain list).
Through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY: the twelve tabulated (steric number, lone pair) cases on their textbook
molecules - CO2 linear, BF3 trigonal planar, SO2 bent, CH4 tetrahedral at arccos(-1/3), NH3 trigonal pyramidal,
H2O bent, PCl5 trigonal bipyramidal, SF4 seesaw, ClF3 T-shaped, SF6 octahedral, BrF5 square pyramidal, XeF4
square planar. The VSEPR model and its measured lone-pair angles are CITED; the tetrahedral angle is a theorem
of geometry; the assignments are SEALED. Idempotent.

sticks.question: Molecular geometry - VSEPR shapes and bond angles, sealed
sticks.statement: A molecule's shape follows from its steric number and lone pairs: electron domains repel to the arrangement of greatest separation, and the bond angle is that arrangement's angle.
references: R. J. Gillespie & R. S. Nyholm, Inorganic stereochemistry, Q. Rev. Chem. Soc. 11 (1957) 339
CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Structure of free molecules in the gas phase

marks.claim: [CO2, SEALED] Two domains, no lone pairs: linear, 180 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY). Two things repelling on a sphere go to opposite poles.
[BF3, SEALED] Three domains: trigonal planar, 120 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY).
[SO2, SEALED] Three domains, one a lone pair: bent, about 119 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY). The shape is named by the atoms, the angle set by all three domains.

[CH4, SEALED] Four domains: tetrahedral, 109.47 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY) - arccos(-1/3), the angle from the centre of a regular tetrahedron to two vertices. Pure geometry, no chemistry in it: the geometry stick's 'Cat:Dog' pair, two domains confirming one number.

[NH3, SEALED] Four domains, one lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, 107 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY). The lone pair takes more room than a bond and squeezes the H-N-H angle below tetrahedral.

[H2O, SEALED] Four domains, two lone pairs: bent, 104.5 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY). Two lone pairs squeeze harder - the angle that makes water polar, and so a solvent, and so the medium of life.
[PCl5, SEALED] Five domains: trigonal bipyramidal (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY) - two angles, 90 and 120, so no single bond angle is claimed; the verifier refuses one.
[SF4, SEALED] Five domains, one lone pair: seesaw (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY) - the lone pair takes an equatorial site, where it crowds two neighbours at 90 deg instead of three.
[ClF3, SEALED] Five domains, two lone pairs: T-shaped (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY).
[SF6, SEALED] Six domains: octahedral, 90 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY).
[BrF5, SEALED] Six domains, one lone pair: square pyramidal (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY).

[XeF4, SEALED] Six domains, two lone pairs: square planar, 90 deg (sealed through molecular_geometry.VSEPR_VERIFY) - the lone pairs take the two axial sites, opposite each other, and the four fluorines lie in a plane. A noble gas with a shape.

[the model, CITED] VSEPR (Gillespie & Nyholm 1957) is a MODEL: electron domains repel and settle at maximum separation, lone pairs repel more than bonds. It works for main-group molecules and fails for many transition-metal ones, so a shape it predicts is inferred, never kept as fact - the measured structure is the fact (CRC tables: H2O 104.5 deg, NH3 106.7 deg). The 180, 120, 90 and 109.47 degree angles are geometry's theorems; the lone-pair angles are measurements the model only approximates.
marks.source: Gillespie & Nyholm, Q. Rev. 11 (1957) 339; CRC Handbook, gas-phase structures

marks.claim: [on the one map] The shape of a molecule is chemistry (card_floor_chemistry: valence, bonding domains) meeting geometry (the geometry stick: the regular polyhedra and their central angles). The tetrahedral angle is the joint: one number, two floors, neither borrowing from the other.
marks.source: the one map; card_floor_chemistry; the geometry stick
